title: NHS Scope 3 2027: What Every Supplier Needs to Know Now
excerpt: From April 2027, all NHS suppliers must publish a Carbon Reduction Plan covering global Scope 1, 2, and all relevant Scope 3 emissions. Here is what you need to do to prepare.
content:
The 2027 Deadline Is Closer Than You Think

From April 2027, the NHS will require all suppliers — regardless of contract value — to publish a comprehensive Carbon Reduction Plan (CRP) that covers global Scope 1, 2, and all relevant Scope 3 emissions. This represents a significant expansion from the current requirements, which apply only to contracts above £5 million per annum.

What Is Scope 3?

Scope 3 emissions are indirect emissions that occur in a company's value chain — both upstream (suppliers, purchased goods) and downstream (use of sold products, end-of-life treatment). For most organisations, Scope 3 accounts for 70–90% of their total carbon emissions, making it the most significant and most challenging category to measure and report.

The NHS Evergreen Framework

The NHS Evergreen Sustainable Supplier Assessment is the mechanism through which the NHS engages suppliers on their sustainability programme. It covers a range of sustainability topics including carbon, waste, water, and social value. From 2027, full Scope 3 reporting will be a mandatory component of Evergreen compliance.

Steps to Take Now

Organisations that act early will be better positioned to win NHS contracts and demonstrate genuine leadership on sustainability. The key steps are: establish a baseline carbon emissions covering all three scopes; identify your most material Scope 3 categories; develop a credible reduction strategy with science-aligned targets; publish your Carbon Reduction Plan in line with PPN006 requirements.

How Net Zero International Can Help

We specialise in helping NHS suppliers navigate the full compliance programme — from baseline carbon accounting through to published, independently verified Carbon Reduction Plans. Contact us today to discuss your requirements.

title: What Is a Life Cycle Assessment and Why Does Your Business Need One?
excerpt: A Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) quantifies the environmental impact of a product or project across its entire life — from raw material extraction to end-of-life disposal. Here is a practical guide to understanding LCAs and their business value.
content:
Understanding Life Cycle Assessment

A Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is a systematic methodology for evaluating the environmental impacts associated with all stages of a product or project's life — from raw material extraction and processing, through manufacture, distribution, and use, to end-of-life disposal or recycling. This cradle-to-grave approach provides a comprehensive picture of environmental performance that goes far beyond simple carbon emissionsing.

The ISO 14040/14044 Framework

LCAs conducted by Net Zero International follow the internationally recognised ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 standards. These standards define the four phases of an LCA: goal and scope definition, inventory analysis, impact assessment, and interpretation. Adherence to these standards ensures that our LCA reports are credible, defensible, and suitable for use in procurement, regulatory, and marketing contexts.

Why Businesses Commission LCAs

Organisations commission LCAs for a variety of strategic and operational reasons. Product manufacturers use LCAs to identify environmental hotspots in their supply chains and inform eco-design decisions. Construction companies use project LCAs to demonstrate embodied carbon performance and meet planning requirements. Businesses seeking to make credible environmental claims — such as carbon neutrality or reduced environmental impact — need an LCA to substantiate those claims.

LCAs and Competitive Advantage

In an increasingly sustainability-conscious market, an LCA report can be a powerful differentiator. It provides the evidence base for environmental product declarations (EPDs), supports green procurement bids, and demonstrates to customers and investors that your environmental commitments are grounded in rigorous science.

title: PPN006 Explained: A Complete Guide for UK Government Suppliers
excerpt: Procurement Policy Note 006 requires UK government suppliers to publish a Carbon Reduction Plan. This guide explains exactly what is required, who is affected, and how to comply.
content:
What Is PPN006?

Procurement Policy Note 006 (PPN006, formerly PPN 06/21) is a UK government policy that requires suppliers bidding for major central government contracts to publish a Carbon Reduction Plan (CRP). The CRP must confirm a commitment to achieving net zero by 2050 and report baseline emissions data covering Scopes 1, 2, and relevant Scope 3 categories.

Who Does PPN006 Apply To?

PPN006 currently applies to suppliers bidding for contracts with a value of £5 million or more per annum with central government departments. However, the NHS has extended these requirements to all suppliers from April 2027, regardless of contract value, making compliance relevant to a much wider range of organisations.

What Must a Carbon Reduction Plan Include?

A compliant CRP must include: a commitment to achieving net zero by 2050 in the UK; a current year and baseline year emissions footprint covering Scopes 1 and 2, and relevant Scope 3 categories; at least five environmental management measures being implemented; and a declaration signed by a director or equivalent senior officer.

The Independent Verification Requirement

One of the most important aspects of PPN006 compliance is the requirement for independent verification of the emissions data included in the CRP. Net Zero International provides independently verified Carbon Reduction Plans that meet the full technical standard set out in the PPN006 guidance.

title: Understanding CSRD: What European Businesses Must Do by 2025
excerpt: The EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) is the most significant expansion of sustainability reporting requirements in European history. Here is what businesses need to know.
content:
What Is the CSRD?

The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) is EU legislation that significantly expands the scope and detail of sustainability reporting requirements for companies operating in Europe. It replaces the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) and introduces mandatory reporting against the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS).

Who Is Affected?

The CSRD applies in phases, starting with large public-interest companies in 2024, expanding to all large companies in 2025, and extending to listed SMEs and non-EU companies with significant EU operations by 2026–2028. Ultimately, it will affect approximately 50,000 companies — a tenfold increase from the NFRD.

What Must Be Reported?

Under the CSRD, companies must report on a wide range of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) topics, including climate change (both transition and physical risks), biodiversity, water, circular economy, and social matters. The climate reporting requirements are closely aligned with the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) framework.

The Double Materiality Principle

A distinctive feature of the CSRD is its double materiality principle, which requires companies to report on both the impact of sustainability issues on the business (financial materiality) and the impact of the business on the environment and society (impact materiality). This represents a more comprehensive approach than purely financial materiality.

title: Net Zero Leaders: Why CPD-Accredited Training Matters for Your Organisation
excerpt: CPD-accredited Net Zero training does more than upskill your team — it demonstrates a credible commitment to professional development in sustainability. Here is why it matters.
content:
The Growing Demand for Net Zero Competence

As net zero commitments move from aspiration to legal requirement, the demand for professionals who genuinely understand carbon accounting, climate science, and sustainability strategy has never been higher. Organisations that invest in structured, accredited training are better positioned to deliver on their commitments — and to demonstrate that capability to clients, investors, and regulators.

What CPD Accreditation Means

CPD (Continuing Professional Development) accreditation from the CPD Certification Service is a recognised mark of quality for professional training. It confirms that the course content, delivery, and learning outcomes meet defined standards of professional development. For participants, CPD-accredited training contributes to their professional development records and is recognised by professional bodies across a wide range of sectors.

The Net Zero Leaders Course

Our Net Zero Leaders course is designed specifically for business leaders, sustainability managers, procurement professionals, and finance teams who need to understand net zero — not just in theory, but in practice. The course covers the science of climate change, the GHG Protocol and carbon accounting methodology, Science-Based Targets, regulatory frameworks including PPN006, SECR, and NHS Evergreen, and practical strategy development.

Online and In-Person Delivery

The course is available as a full-day online session or an in-person workshop for up to 12 participants. We also offer bespoke delivery for single organisations, allowing the content to be tailored to your sector, supply chain, and specific compliance requirements.

title: Scope 3 Emissions: The Complete Guide for Supply Chain Managers
excerpt: Scope 3 emissions typically account for 70-90% of a company's carbon emissions, yet they remain the least understood and most challenging to measure. This guide explains everything you need to know.
content:
What Are Scope 3 Emissions?

The GHG Protocol Corporate Standard divides greenhouse gas emissions into three scopes. Scope 1 covers direct emissions from sources owned or controlled by the company. Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased energy. Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions that occur in a company's value chain — both upstream and downstream.

The 15 Scope 3 Categories

The GHG Protocol defines 15 categories of Scope 3 emissions, spanning upstream activities (purchased goods and services, capital goods, fuel and energy-related activities, upstream transportation, waste, business travel, employee commuting, upstream leased assets) and downstream activities (downstream transportation, processing of sold products, use of sold products, end-of-life treatment, downstream leased assets, franchises, and investments).

Why Scope 3 Matters

For most organisations, Scope 3 emissions represent the vast majority of their total carbon emissions — often 70–90% or more. This means that a net zero strategy that focuses only on Scopes 1 and 2 will fail to address the most significant sources of emissions. Increasingly, regulators, investors, and customers are requiring full Scope 3 disclosure.

The 2027 NHS Requirement

From April 2027, all NHS suppliers must report all relevant Scope 3 emissions as part of their Carbon Reduction Plan. This is a significant step change from current requirements and will require many organisations to undertake a comprehensive Scope 3 assessment for the first time.
author: Net Zero International
